{{Short description|Business cycle indicator}}
{{use dmy dates|date=June 2024}}

The '''Aruoba-Diebold-Scotti Business Conditions Index''' ("ADS Index" ) is a coincident [[business cycle]] [[Economic indicator|indicator]] used in [[macroeconomics]] in the United States. The index measures business activity, which may be correlated with periods of expansion and contraction in the [[Economy of the United States|economy]]. The primary and novel function of the ADS index stems from its use of high-frequency economic data and subsequent high-frequency updating, opposed to the traditionally highly-lagged and infrequently-published macroeconomic data such as [[Gross domestic product|GDP]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Aruoba |first1=S. Boragan |last2=Diebold |first2=Francis |last3=Scotti |first3=Chiara |date=2009 |title=Real-Time Measurement of Business Conditions |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.3386/w14349 |journal=Journal of Business & Economic Statistics |location=Cambridge, MA |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=417–427 |doi=10.1198/jbes.2009.07205 |s2cid=219594039|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Giannone |first1=Domenico |last2=Reichlin |first2=Lucrezia |last3=Small |first3=David |date=2008 |title=Nowcasting: The real-time informational content of macroeconomic data |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304393208000652 |journal=Journal of Monetary Economics |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=665–676 |doi=10.1016/j.jmoneco.2008.05.010 |issn=0304-3932|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Croushore |first=Dean |date=2008 |title=Frontiers of Real-Time Data Analysis |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.1118356 |journal=SSRN Electronic Journal |doi=10.2139/ssrn.1118356 |issn=1556-5068 |s2cid=145330221}}</ref>

== Development ==
The ADS index was first introduced by the authors, including [[Francis X. Diebold|Francis Diebold]], in March 2007 and published in October 2008, but the index is retroactively calculated back to March 1960.<ref name=":3">{{Cite report |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w27482.pdf |title=Real-Time Real Economic Activity: Exiting the Great Recession and Entering the Pandemic Recession |last=Diebold |first=Francis |date=July 2020 |publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |issue=w27482 |doi=10.3386/w27482 |location=Cambridge, MA |pages=2–3 |language=en |id=27482 |series=NBER Working Paper}}</ref>

While other economic nowcasting often estimates GDP or [[inflation]],<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Banbura |first1=M. |title=Handbook of Economic Forecasting |last2=Giannone |first2=D. |last3=Modugno |first3=M. |last4=Reichlin |first4=L. |year=2013 |editor-last=Elliott |editor-first=G. |volume=2, Part A |pages=195–237 |chapter=Nowcasting and the Real-Time Data Flow |doi=10.1016/B978-0-444-53683-9.00004-9 |hdl=10419/153997 |isbn=978-0-444-53683-9 |editor-last2=Timmermann |editor-first2=A. |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780444536839000049}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Nowcasting Report - Methodology |url=https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/policy/nowcast/methodology.html |website=Federal Reserve Bank of New York}}</ref> the ADS index exists as a stand-alone series. This is in part due to the business cycle not tied to a single variable, such as GDP, employment, or [[industrial production]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lucas |first=R. E. |year=1977 |title=Understanding Business Cycles |journal=Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy |volume=5 |pages=7–29 |doi=10.1016/0167-2231(77)90002-1}}</ref> Instead, business cycle theory suggests an underlying [[Factor analysis|factor]] that moves each of these series. The ADS index estimates that unobserved factor.

The index itself is the principal factor produced by a [[Dynamic factor|dynamic factor model]]. As standard for such models, it is cast in [[State-space representation|state space]] and estimated using [[maximum likelihood estimation]] methods.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stock |first1=J. H. |first2=M. W. |last2=Watson |year=1989 |chapter=New Indexes of Coincident and Leading Economic Indicators |editor-first=O. J. |editor-last=Blanchard |editor-first2=S. |editor-last2=Fischer |title=NBER Macroeconomics Annual |publisher=MIT Press |pages=351–393 |isbn=0-262-02296-6 |chapter-url=http://www.nber.org/chapters/c10968}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Durbin |first1=J. |last2=Koopman |first2=S.J. |year=2001 |title=Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods |location=Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press|bibcode=2001tsas.book.....D }}</ref> A [[Kalman filter]] handles the missing data that arises from using a mix of frequencies of input data.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bańbura |first1=Marta |last2=Modugno |first2=Michele |date=2012 |title=Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Factor Models on Datasets with Arbitrary Pattern of Missing Data |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jae.2306 |journal=Journal of Applied Econometrics |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=133–160 |doi=10.1002/jae.2306 |s2cid=14231301 |hdl-access=free |hdl=10419/153623}}</ref> For example, a daily series such as [[Yield curve|term premium]] sets the entire model to be daily. Unemployment data is collected monthly, though, so all days between releases are treated as missing data.<ref name=":0" />

The factor deals with the de-meaned growth rate of business activity, such that it is (a) centered on 0, and (b) measures deviation from average growth.<ref name=":3" /> Thus, an ADS score of 0 indicates completely average growth, positive values indicate greater than average, and negative less than average.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last1=Doelp |first1=Patrick |last2=Stark |first2=Tom |title=Aruoba-Diebold-Scotti Business Conditions Index |url=https://www.philadelphiafed.org/surveys-and-data/real-time-data-research/ads |website=Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia}}</ref>

== Data ==
The ADS initially used just four input series to estimate the unobserved factor: GDP, Employment, Initial Claims, and Slope (of daily term structure). However, removing this last term yielded no loss in model accuracy. This demonstrates that more is not always better. The weekly initial claims in unemployment was helpful, though.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aruoba |first1=S. Boragan |last2=Diebold |first2=Francis |last3=Scotti |first3=Chiara |date=2009 |title=Real-Time Measurement of Business Conditions |journal=American Statistical Association |location=Cambridge, MA |pages=15 |doi=10.3386/w14349 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Currently, the ADS relies on the following data:<ref name=":4" />

* [[Jobless claims|Initial jobless claims]] (weekly)
* Payroll employment (monthly)
* [[Industrial production]] (monthly)
* [[Personal income in the United States|Real personal income]], less [[transfer payment]]s (monthly)
* Real manufacturing and trade sales (monthly)
* Real [[Gross domestic product|GDP]] (monthly)

== Usage ==
The ADS is currently maintained by the [[Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia]], where it is made publicly available.<ref name=":4" />  The index updates with the release of new data upon which it relies, usually eight times a month.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Economic Release Schedule |url=http://www.philadelphiafed.org/calendar-of-events |access-date=2020-12-16 |website=Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia}}</ref>

The index does not predict an economic recession. Rather than leading the business cycle, it [[Coincident indicator|coincides]].<ref name=":0" /> While it may have limited use in high-frequency finance, it serves a purpose in aiding monetary and fiscal policy by providing a quantitative measure of the current state of the economy.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />
